title: Antisymmetric Wavefunctions can be Represented by Slater Determinants
lead: Helium's two electrons, in the ground state and in the first excited state, show how antisymmetric wavefunctions are built from spin-orbitals. The Slater determinant turns that construction into a recipe for any number of electrons.
objectives: Understand how the Pauli Exclusion principle affects the electronic configuration of mulit-electron atoms
Understand how determinantal wavefunctions (Slater determinents) ensure the proper symmetry to electron permutation required by Pauli Exclusion Principle.
Connect the electron permutation symmetry requirement to multi-electron wavefunctions to the Aufbau principle taught in general chemistry courses
notes: Written by Theodore Zielinski and shared under CC BY-NC-SA 4.0; the book gives no credit for Figures 8.6.1 and 8.6.2, which are shown under the page's licence.
exercise_notes: Exercises 8.6.1, 8.6.2 and 8.6.3A and their answers are the book's, with corrections under 8.6.2 and 8.6.3A; Exercise 8.6.3B, an open question the book leaves unanswered, has an AI answer. Bloom levels and concept tags were chosen by AI.

exercises.prompt:
Is this linear combination of spin-orbitals

$$ | \psi (\mathbf{r}_1, \mathbf{r}_2) \rangle = \dfrac {1}{\sqrt {2}} [ \varphi _{1s\alpha}(\mathbf{r}_1) \varphi _{1s\beta}( \mathbf{r}_2) + \varphi _{1s\alpha}( \mathbf{r}_2) \varphi _{1s\beta}(\mathbf{r}_1)] $$

symmetric or antisymmetric with respect to permutation of the two electrons?
Write and expand the Slater determinant for the ground-state $\mathrm{Li}$ atom.

answer.solution:
Slater determinant for $\mathrm{Li}$ atom:

$$ \psi(1,2,3)=\frac{1}{\sqrt{6}} \operatorname{det}\left(\begin{array}{ccc} {\varphi _{1s} \alpha(1)} & {\varphi _{1s} \beta(1)} & {\varphi _{2s} \alpha(1)} \\ \varphi _{1s} \alpha(2) & {\varphi _{1s} \beta(2)} & {\varphi _{2s} \alpha(2)} \\ {\varphi _{1s} \alpha(3)} & {\varphi _{1s} \beta(3)} & {\varphi _{2s} \alpha(3)} \end{array}\right) $$

Expansion of Slater determinant:

$$ \psi(1,2,3)=\frac{1}{\sqrt{6}}[\varphi _{1s} \alpha(1) \varphi _{1s} \beta(2) \varphi _{2s} \alpha(3)-\varphi _{1s} \alpha(1) \varphi _{1s} \beta(3) \varphi _{2s} \alpha(2)+ \varphi _{1s} \alpha(3) \varphi _{1s} \beta(1) \varphi _{2s} \alpha(2) - \varphi _{1s} \alpha(3) \varphi _{1s} \beta(2) \varphi _{1s} \alpha(1)+ \varphi _{1s} \alpha(2) \varphi _{1s} \beta(3) \varphi _{2s} \alpha(3) ] $$

Note that this is also a valid ground state wavefunction

$$ \psi(1,2,3)=\frac{1}{\sqrt{6}} \operatorname{det}\left(\begin{array}{ccc} {\varphi _{1s} \alpha(1)} & {\varphi _{1s} \beta(1)} & {\varphi _{2s} \beta(1)} \\ \varphi _{1s} \alpha(2) & {\varphi _{1s} \beta(2)} & {\varphi _{2s} \beta(2)} \\ {\varphi _{1s} \alpha(3)} & {\varphi _{1s} \beta(3)} & {\varphi _{2s} \beta(3)} \end{array}\right) $$

What is the difference between these two wavefunctions?

exercises.prompt: Write the Slater determinant for the $1s^12s^1$ excited state orbital configuration of the helium atom.

answer.solution:
Since there are 2 electrons in question, the Slater determinant should have 2 rows and 2 columns exactly. Additionally, this means the normalization constant is $1/\sqrt{2}$.

Each element of the determinant is a different combination of the spatial component and the spin component of the $1 s^{1} 2 s^{1}$ atomic orbitals

$$ \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\left[\begin{array}{cc} {\varphi _{1_s}(1) \alpha(1)} & {\varphi {2_s}(1) \beta(1)} \\ {\varphi {1_s}(2) \alpha(2)} & {\varphi {2_s}(2) \beta(2)} \end{array}\right] $$

exercises.prompt: Critique the energy level diagram and shorthand electron configuration notation from the perspective of the indistinguishability criterion. Can you imagine a way to represent the wavefunction expressed as a Slater determinant in a schematic or shorthand notation that more accurately represents the electrons? (This is not a solved problem!)

answer.hint: In a Slater determinant, which spin-orbitals does electron 1 appear in?
answer.solution:
A stick diagram puts one arrow, read as one particular electron with one particular spin, on one particular orbital. The indistinguishability criterion forbids exactly that: in a Slater determinant every electron appears in every column, so no electron belongs to any spin-orbital, and each spin-orbital holds one electron's worth of charge shared among all the electrons. The diagram also suggests that every state is one arrangement of arrows, yet configurations 1 and 4 of Figure 8.6.2 never occur alone, only as the combinations $\psi_1$ and $\psi_3$.

A shorthand closer to the determinant lists the occupied spin-orbitals with no electron labels at all, such as $|1s\alpha\, 2s\beta|$ for the determinant of Equation 8.6.10, and writes a state that needs two determinants as their sum, $\psi_1 = (|1s\alpha\, 2s\beta| - |1s\beta\, 2s\alpha|)/\sqrt{2}$. A diagram could do the same by drawing filled spin-orbitals instead of labelled arrows, and joining the diagrams of a combination with their signs. Labels for the whole atom, such as the term symbols of Section 8.8, go further and name a state by its total spin instead of by single electrons.

footnotes.html: Normalized, $\psi_3$ carries $\tfrac{1}{2}$, like $\psi_1$, and $\psi_4$ carries $\tfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}$, like $\psi_2$: each bracket of two terms brings a factor $\tfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}$.
The functions that had to be combined are $\psi_1$ and $\psi_3$ of Equation 8.6.6.

The first line lacks the normalization: $|\psi_1\rangle = (|\phi_a\rangle - |\phi_c\rangle)/\sqrt{2}$, which the second line's $\tfrac{1}{2}$ already includes. Likewise $|\psi_3\rangle = (|\phi_a\rangle + |\phi_c\rangle)/\sqrt{2}$.

A $3 \times 3$ determinant expands into six terms. Two printed terms are wrong (the fourth ends in $\varphi_{1s}\alpha(1)$ and the fifth in $\varphi_{2s}\alpha(3)$, where $\varphi_{2s}\alpha(1)$ belongs in both), and $-\varphi_{1s}\alpha(2)\varphi_{1s}\beta(1)\varphi_{2s}\alpha(3)$ is missing. In full: $\psi(1,2,3) = \frac{1}{\sqrt{6}}[\varphi_{1s}\alpha(1)\varphi_{1s}\beta(2)\varphi_{2s}\alpha(3) - \varphi_{1s}\alpha(1)\varphi_{1s}\beta(3)\varphi_{2s}\alpha(2) - \varphi_{1s}\alpha(2)\varphi_{1s}\beta(1)\varphi_{2s}\alpha(3) + \varphi_{1s}\alpha(2)\varphi_{1s}\beta(3)\varphi_{2s}\alpha(1) + \varphi_{1s}\alpha(3)\varphi_{1s}\beta(1)\varphi_{2s}\alpha(2) - \varphi_{1s}\alpha(3)\varphi_{1s}\beta(2)\varphi_{2s}\alpha(1)]$.

The key leaves the question open. The two determinants differ only in the spin of the 2s electron, $\alpha$ in the first and $\beta$ in the second: they are the two spin states, $M_S = +\tfrac{1}{2}$ and $-\tfrac{1}{2}$, of the same ground level, with the same energy.

A determinant is written between vertical bars, $\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\begin{vmatrix} \varphi_{1s}(1)\alpha(1) & \varphi_{2s}(1)\beta(1) \\ \varphi_{1s}(2)\alpha(2) & \varphi_{2s}(2)\beta(2) \end{vmatrix}$, as in Equation 8.6.10; square brackets denote the matrix itself. This is configuration 1 of Figure 8.6.2, and the determinants of the other three configurations (Equations 8.6.11 to 8.6.13) answer the question as well.
